card: Admiralty House, London, with the President at the other end of the private line. Eight days, 21 to 28 October · 10 decisions. The ally was only informed, and you are that ally’s sole counterpart.
intro: You are Maurice Harold Macmillan, 68, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. You served as an officer in the First World War and were wounded three times; you were one of the few who withheld your vote from the government in the Munich division of 1938; and at Suez in 1956, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, you watched a British policy without America fall apart. In 1959 you spent ten days with Khrushchev in Moscow, and since 1961 you have been linked to Kennedy by teleprinter and telephone. Your ambassador in Washington, Ormsby-Gore, is an old friend of the Kennedy family; your foreign secretary, Lord Home, is quiet and firm. You cannot move missiles. What you can move is words: private words to the President, public words in the House of Commons, letters to Khrushchev. Which way those words tip the scales in Washington is your decision. On 22 October Britain was informed after the decision had been made, and on 28 October your letter was delivered in Moscow at the same hour as Khrushchev’s broadcast. Relive the eight days in between: what you could have done, and what you did not do. Britain stayed on summer time until the early hours of 28 October, so it was five hours ahead of Washington and two hours behind Moscow.

HM-01.time: Evening (afternoon in Washington, night in Moscow)
HM-01.place: The Prime Minister’s office, Admiralty House, Whitehall, London
HM-01.title: A Private Message on the Teleprinter

map.caption: From the night of 22 October, Macmillan and Kennedy talked by telephone and cable almost every night.

HM-01.clock: About 16 hours until Ambassador Bruce’s noon call

telegram.at: Sent 5:22 p.m., received 5:50 p.m., 20 October 1962 (Washington time)
telegram.subject: Cuba
telegram.text: My telegram No. 2623 of 20 October reported present pressure on the President to take action over Cuba. / You should know that concern within the Administration has been growing as a result of the latest intelligence assessments of the Soviet build-up. This anxiety springs not only from the increase in numbers of weapons and military personnel but from reports that the types of weapons introduced may not be wholly defensive. / 2. In the last few days there has been much activity in the State Department and the Pentagon suggesting that contingency plans for military action of some kind in connection with Cuba are being brought to readiness, and at the President’s request the appreciation of the situation is being urgently brought up to date. / 3. Sir Hugh Stephenson will report fully to the Foreign Secretary as soon as he returns to London.

HM-01.event: On Friday 19 October in Washington, Cline of the CIA showed the Cuban photographs to British intelligence officials (Stephenson, chairman of the Joint Intelligence Committee, and Strong, director of the Joint Intelligence Bureau). On Saturday 20 October the President cut short his campaigning in Chicago, pleading a cold, and returned to Washington. That evening two telegrams from Ambassador Ormsby-Gore reached London, and at lunch on Sunday the 21st the ambassador was called alone to the White House to sit down with the President.
HM-01.scene: Admiralty House is quiet on Sunday evening. No. 10 Downing Street has been under reconstruction since 1960, so for two years you have worked from these temporary quarters. The Foreign Secretary, Lord Home, is here, and your private secretary, de Zulueta, comes in carrying a box of telegrams. Ormsby-Gore had warned that a “message of the utmost importance” would soon arrive, and after dark the President’s personal message came through on the teleprinter. It speaks of intelligence gained from photographic reconnaissance and of an “extremely dangerous and aggressive” Soviet step, and says Ambassador Bruce will come at noon tomorrow to explain in detail. It does not say whether it will be a blockade or an air strike, or what America means to do. You are 68. You were wounded three times in the First World War, and in 1938 you withheld your vote from the government in the Munich division. In 1959 you spent ten days with Khrushchev in Moscow, and you believe you know what he wants over Berlin. The talks on entry into the Common Market have reached a critical point in Brussels, and since the sweeping reshuffle of July, Gaitskell of the Labour Party has been hounding you. Lord Home asks whether you will tell the Cabinet, or wait until Bruce has come.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (ambassador in Washington, reporting his conversation with the President on 21 October)
voices.text: The President said that the situation in Cuba had changed completely in the past week. Extensive photographic reconnaissance by U-2 aircraft had revealed that Cuba was being equipped with two types of offensive medium-range missiles. The fixed type was estimated to have a range of about 2,000 miles, the mobile type about 1,500 miles. He was not very clear about numbers, but thought there were already between 30 and 40 on the island and more on the way by ship.

Prime Minister, whatever the Americans do, Berlin lies behind it. We all knew Khrushchev meant to come to New York in November and bargain over Berlin. Cuba will be his stake in that bargain. The Cabinet should be told once we know what the American decision is. Until then it would be better to keep it to you, me and the Permanent Under-Secretary.

The President’s message says only that Ambassador Bruce will explain at noon tomorrow. The text of the speech has not come yet. From what Sir David Ormsby-Gore says, two courses were considered, an air strike and a blockade, and he advised the blockade. You could also speak to the President directly tonight on the private line.

choices.text: Keep the secret between yourself, Lord Home and the Permanent Under-Secretary, and reply to the President after hearing Ambassador Bruce’s briefing at noon
choices.why: Adding your voice once the decision is made does the alliance no harm
choices.after: You asked Lord Home to come back in the morning, and told de Zulueta to circulate nothing to the Cabinet Office. Overnight Ormsby-Gore’s long telegram No. 2636 comes in, and you learn that the President asked the ambassador whether he favored an air strike or a blockade. The first question Britain was asked was one whose answer had already been settled.

choices.text: Send the President a message at once on the private line, urging him to confront Khrushchev with the evidence and give him a private ultimatum before any public announcement
choices.why: A private ultimatum leaves the other side a way out that a public confrontation does not
choices.after: The message went to Washington at 11 p.m. No answer came. At noon the next day Ambassador Bruce brought the President’s letter, along with word that the heart of the announcement had already been decided. Your advice came a day too late, and Washington merely put it on the record.

choices.text: Call the senior Cabinet ministers together tonight to warn them of possible American military action, and review in advance the arrangements for British shipping and for Berlin
choices.why: The British government must be ready before it is pulled along by the American decision
choices.after: At 10 p.m. the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Maudling, the Minister of Defense, Thorneycroft, and Lord Home gathered. There was little to go on, so the meeting was short. The next day Ormsby-Gore’s telegram contained a passage saying the President had wanted “only the Prime Minister and his closest advisers” to know, and Washington soon learned that there had been a night meeting in London.

note.text: No. 10 Downing Street was under reconstruction from 1960 to 1963, so Macmillan worked from Admiralty House. Macmillan was wounded in the hand at Loos in 1915 and twice on the Somme in 1916 (in the pelvis on 15 September). Macmillan’s reply of 22 October (222308Z) said the text of the President’s speech had “just come over our teleprinter,” and the text did arrive over the British line before it came through the American embassy. When the line was installed, and what kind of line it was, has not been established. The original of Kennedy’s personal message of the night of 21 October is document 3 of the NSA briefing book; the scan is poor, so the text gives only its gist.

HM-02.time: Noon to 7 p.m. (7 a.m.–2 p.m. in Washington)
HM-02.place: The Prime Minister’s study, Admiralty House
HM-02.title: Life Goes On Somehow
HM-02.clock: 12 hours until the President’s broadcast (midnight in London)

telegram.no: State Department telegram No. 2269 to Embassy London (transmitting the President’s letter)
telegram.at: Sent 12:17 a.m., 22 October 1962 (Washington); delivered 10 a.m. London
telegram.subject: Soviet offensive missiles in Cuba
telegram.text: Dear Friend: / Incontrovertible military evidence from photographic reconnaissance has established that the Soviets have already installed offensive nuclear missiles in Cuba, and some of them may already be operational. / I shall make a public statement at 1900 Washington time this evening, and Ambassador Bruce will bring you a draft with this message. Details may change, but the heart of the matter and the means of response have been decided. / It is my clear view that these missiles must be removed. The purpose of the quarantine, effective at once, is to prevent the introduction of further Soviet missiles and to lead to the removal of those already there. / I wanted you to be the first to know. This is a solemn moment for both our countries, indeed for the fate of the whole world. / I need not point out to you the possible relation of this secret and dangerous move on the part of Khrushchev to Berlin. We shall have to prepare together for a time of testing. / We are calling for an emergency meeting of the Security Council, and Ambassador Stevenson will introduce a resolution calling for the withdrawal of missile bases and offensive weapons from Cuba under UN supervision. I hope you will instruct your representative in New York to give it active support.

HM-02.event: At 10 a.m. on 22 October Ambassador Bruce brought the President’s letter, and at noon he came back with Cooper of the CIA and spread out the photographs: SS-4 launchers at San Cristóbal, IRBM construction at Guanajay, Il-28 bombers still in their shipping crates at San Julián. The same day Acheson gave de Gaulle the same briefing in Paris, and Ambassador Dowling gave it to Adenauer in Bonn. The promised draft of the speech did not come. The American embassy telephoned the State Department for more than four hours, and only at 7 p.m. did Bruce see the text, which he received from the British government after it came in over the British private line.
HM-02.scene: You looked at the photographs for only a few seconds. If the President was convinced, you said, that was enough. While Cooper recited the Soviet offensive strength, you remarked, as if to yourself, that the British had lived for years within range of Soviet nuclear weapons and had got along somehow, and that the Americans would do the same once the first shock had passed; then, worried that it sounded callous, you added a long explanation. When Lord Home came in, the talk turned to policy. A blockade will be hard to enforce, and UN support will not be easy to win. You even wondered aloud whether it would have been better to confront Khrushchev with the evidence and give him a private ultimatum. The two of you listed the likely Soviet replies: blocking access to Berlin, harassing the bases in Turkey, and playing for time by proposing a meeting to the President. In the evening the text of the speech arrived, and you dictate your reply to the President. At the other end of the private line, the President is holding a meeting of the National Security Council.

voices.text: Life goes on somehow.

Prime Minister, the President wanted you to be the first to know. I was briefed myself only at midnight, when I boarded Mr. Acheson’s plane at Greenham Common. I’m told there was a fierce argument in Washington between those who wanted to wipe out the bases and those who wanted to take time, and that the side for taking time won. I will bring you the text of the speech as soon as it arrives.

A blockade that stops and searches the ships of every nation on the high seas in peacetime will be hard to defend in law. The international lawyers will fasten on that. But the ground must be not precedent but the unprecedented conditions of the nuclear age. And if Khrushchev comes to a conference, he will try to trade Cuba for Berlin. That must be prevented at all costs.

I said that I thought the first course he had outlined had very serious drawbacks. Few people outside the United States would consider that the provocation given by Cuba was serious enough to justify an American air strike. Of the two alternatives he had put to me, I would therefore definitely favor the second.

choices.text: Pledge full support in the Security Council, but send a reply asking for the legal grounds and warning of the “dilemma of being the first to fire” and of the danger of a bargain over Berlin
choices.why: Support without conditions and worries in private: that is the courtesy owed an ally
choices.after: The reply reached the White House before 8 p.m. (before 3 p.m. in Washington). Rusk read it out at the 3 p.m. (Washington) meeting of the National Security Council, saying it was not a bad first reaction to news of the blockade, and adding that, happily, the British prime minister had thought of nothing the Americans had not. There and then the President called the message “the best argument for doing nothing.”

choices.text: Formally advise the President on the private line to put off the broadcast by a day and first send Khrushchev a private ultimatum with the photographs
choices.why: The lesson learned since 1938: in an open confrontation, neither side can easily back down
choices.after: The reply went out at 7:30 p.m. Washington’s answer was short: the heart of the statement had been decided, and the congressional leaders were already at the White House. Your advice was not read out at the National Security Council, and at midnight the President broadcast as planned.

choices.text: Tell the President that Britain’s tradition of freedom of the seas does not allow it to support searching ships in peacetime, and hint that it will abstain on the resolution in the Security Council
choices.why: Britain is under no obligation to add its signature to America’s unilateral action
choices.after: The reply went out at 11 p.m. An hour later the private line rang. The President asked whether you knew what a British abstention would mean, and you answered that it was a question of law. The call was short. The next morning there were demonstrators outside the American embassy in Grosvenor Square, and Washington’s protest had arrived in Whitehall.

note.text: Macmillan’s reply (White House receipt number 222308Z) pledged full support in the Security Council, asked for the legal grounds, and warned of the “dilemma of being the first to fire,” of retaliation in Berlin, and of a Cuba-for-Berlin bargain at a conference. Kennedy’s answer, CAP5495-62, replied that doing nothing would be more dangerous for Berlin. 222308Z is the time at which the White House Situation Room passed the cable to the State Department (23:08 Universal Time, 0:08 on the 23rd in London, received at State 19:43); the message itself is recorded as “just received” when the National Security Council met at 3 p.m. (Washington) on 22 October (FRUS XI d41). The only other courses actually considered on the British side on 22 October were the “private ultimatum” remark recorded by Cooper and the legal question of freedom of the seas that Ormsby-Gore raised with the President; abstention was not considered.
note.src: NSA #812 Doc 7·8; FRUS XI d41; Supp d353·d409

pressure.title: A Few Seconds with the Photographs
pressure.text: You looked at the photographs for only a few seconds and said that if the President was convinced, that was enough. What came out first was that the British had lived for years within range of Soviet nuclear weapons and got along somehow, and you had to add a long explanation in case it sounded callous. At Suez in 1956, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, you saw how an ally collapses once America turns its back on it, and in the six years since you have staked your premiership on rebuilding the relationship with Washington. That the prime minister of the country with that relationship was told only after the decision lies beneath every word spoken this afternoon. Some read your musing aloud about confronting Khrushchev with the evidence and a private ultimatum as the reflex of a man who spent ten days with him in Moscow in 1959. Whatever you write in your reply, any path on which Britain does not stand beside America in the Security Council leads, for you, back to Suez.

HM-03.time: 12:30 a.m. (7:30 p.m. on the 22nd in Washington, 2:30 a.m. on the 23rd in Moscow)
HM-03.place: Admiralty House, at the private-line telephone
HM-03.title: The First Night Call
HM-03.clock: About 24 hours until the blockade proclamation is signed (evening of the 23rd, Washington)

telegram.cc: Duty officer, Executive Secretariat, Department of State
telegram.subject: Reply to the Prime Minister’s message 222308Z
telegram.text: Dear Friend: Let me say first that I am sorry the draft of my statement reached you so late. On such occasions we shall have to use our own teleprinter. / The legal basis rests in the first instance on the Rio Treaty, but your point about the wider issues of the nuclear age is right, and I believe a strong case can be made on it. / I fully recognize the dangers you rightly point out, but we also had to weigh the effect of doing nothing in the face of so clear and deep a Soviet challenge. I am aware of the special danger of a riposte in Berlin, but in the larger view I believe that doing nothing would be far more dangerous to our position in that outpost. / US naval commanders are instructed to use the minimum of force. But I know of no sure way out of the problem of the first shot. The best basic course is firmness, and firmness now.

HM-03.event: At midnight London time the President went on television to reveal the Soviet missiles in Cuba and declare a naval quarantine. It was 2 a.m. in Moscow and 6 p.m. in Havana. An hour before the speech Rusk handed Ambassador Dobrynin a letter for Khrushchev, and the Soviet ambassador left stony-faced. Havana had ordered general mobilization before the speech, and in New York the United States, the Soviet Union and Cuba all asked for a meeting of the Security Council. After the speech, demonstrations began in Grosvenor Square. Thirty minutes later, at 12:30 a.m., the private line rang.
HM-03.scene: In the study there are only you, de Zulueta and a secretary taking shorthand. The voice at the other end is quick and tired. Had the Soviets been allowed to arm Cuba in secret, the President says, the whole of Latin America would have been shaken, and every word about Berlin would have been doubted. You ask slowly: what is the blockade meant to do? Will he occupy Cuba and have done with it, or will it simply drag on? The President answers that an occupation would take days and the preparations could not be hidden, and that the blockade does not extend to oil so that the same thing is not done to them in Berlin. You say that in your long experience Britain’s weakness has been failing to act with enough force at the start, but that once you are drawn into a conference, all the cards are in the other man’s hand, and you hope America holds plenty of cards. Then you ask whether the next step is a conference or warlike measures. The President says an invasion would take seven days, and that he will not undertake one before talking to you again. How you end this call will become the British government’s first official stance.

voices.text: What are you going to do with the blockade? Are you going to occupy Cuba and have done with it, or is it just going to drag on?
voices.src: PREM 11/3689, Record of a Conversation 12:30 a.m. 23 Oct 1962 (NSA #812 Doc 9)

voices.text: In my long experience, the weakness of the British position has always shown itself when we have not acted with sufficient strength at the start.

voices.who: John F. Kennedy (American record, summary memorandum)
voices.text: We are trying to increase the pressure in a way that avoids a third world war. It may come to that in the end, but we cannot accept what Khrushchev has done.

voices.who: John F. Kennedy (American record, summary memorandum)
voices.text: An invasion may become necessary. It takes seven days to mobilize the forces required. In any case we will not invade without talking to you again.

choices.text: Suggest waiting for the Soviet reaction, and promise always to move together through the Ormsby-Gore channel. Tell Bruce that the British government is with them
choices.why: On this night all Britain can do is let it be known that it stands alongside
choices.after: You said he must have had a very hard time, that you were sorry for all his troubles, and that you had been through it yourself; then you put down the receiver. At 1 a.m. you telephoned Ambassador Bruce to say the British government was with them. The ambassador wrote in his diary that the Prime Minister had been warm and friendly. At the same hour the police in Grosvenor Square were pushing back the demonstrators.

choices.text: Saying that letting it drag on is the greatest danger, press the President to occupy Cuba and finish it as soon as the forces are assembled
choices.why: Experience: Britain’s weakness was always failing to use enough force at the start
choices.after: The President was silent for a moment, then said he wished he had the force in hand tonight, but it would take a week. If it looked wise by the weekend, he added, it could be done. Only after you had put down the receiver did it sink in what you had said, for you knew what the Joint Intelligence Committee would say about Berlin in the morning.

choices.text: Propose that if the Soviets respond with words, you at once call for a conference and a package settlement, adding that Britain could host it
choices.why: The memory of the 1959 Moscow visit: when you hold few cards, it pays to open the game early
choices.after: The President answered that he could not tell what exchange a conference might lead to, but that getting the missiles out was the aim of his policy. He made no reply to the offer of a British venue. The next day Ormsby-Gore sent a telegram explaining what that silence meant: Washington felt it was not yet time to speak of a conference.

note.text: There are two records of this call. The American record (FRUS XI d45) summarizes only the President’s remarks and leaves the Prime Minister’s blank as “PM spoke.” The British record (PREM 11/3689) keeps both sides in dialogue form. Together they show that the blockade was not extended to oil (POL) in order to avoid a “riposte” in Berlin. The President’s reply, CAP5495-62, has gaps in the scan, so some letters have been restored from context, and its sending time (DTG) is illegible. The time of the call follows the heading of the British record (12:30 a.m., 23 October).
note.src: FRUS XI d45; PREM 11/3689 (NSA #812 Doc 8·9); Supp d353

pressure.title: A Man Who Has Been Through It
pressure.text: In the 12:30 a.m. call you told the President he must have had a very hard time, and that you had been through such troubles yourself. You were thinking of Suez. The lesson you drew from it is that Britain failed to act with enough force at the start, and once drawn into a conference found all the cards in the other side’s hand. That is why you asked whether he would occupy Cuba and finish it or let it drag on, though the question can also be read as urging him toward war. You are 68 and the President is 45, and the voice at the other end is quick and tired. Tonight it will be settled whether your parting words reach Ambassador Bruce as a sign that the British government stands with America, or leave another path open.
pressure.src: PREM 11/3689, Record of a Conversation 12:30 a.m. 23 Oct 1962 (NSA #812 Doc 9); FRUS XI d45

HM-04.time: 6 p.m. (1 p.m. in Washington, 9 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-04.place: London: Admiralty House and the American ambassador’s residence, after the Cabinet meeting
HM-04.title: The Photographs and the Opposition
HM-04.clock: 21 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (3 p.m. on the 24th, London)

telegram.subject: Cuba: reply to Prime Minister’s telegram
telegram.text: Clear from talk with President that he neither expects nor intends present measures to lead to US occupation of Cuba. He went so far as to say no such good pretext for invasion would come again once this chance passed. Blockade also narrowed: P.O.L. not to be stopped for the present. / 2. President named no meeting with Khrushchev but plainly hopes crisis can be resolved by negotiation and discussion. Said with great seriousness that existence of nuclear weapons made a safe and rational world impossible. Bases in Turkey and other IRBM bases now practically useless, and doubtful they were ever a good plan. Cannot tell whether deal on mutual closing of bases politically possible, but sees no objection from military point of view. / These remarks so frank that President will repeat them to no one but his brother Bobby. You will understand how important that none of this become known to any American, President himself included. / 5. Bobby Kennedy telephoned last night: only lukewarm reaction President has had from allies came from Canada.

HM-04.event: Crossing point ④. At 10 a.m. on 23 October the Joint Intelligence Committee heard Cooper’s briefing. White of MI6 and the committee’s chairman, Stephenson, came to the same judgment: Khrushchev had meant to present a fait accompli in November and bargain it against Berlin and overseas bases, and his retaliation would most likely be to block access to Berlin. The Cabinet met in the morning (CC(62)61), and Lord Home agreed to make a speech that evening supporting the United States. In Moscow, at 10 a.m. (7 a.m. in London), the Presidium ordered the ships carrying missiles among those bound for Cuba to turn back, but Washington would not know it until the next morning. In New York the Security Council’s 1022nd meeting opens at 4 p.m. (9 p.m. in London).
HM-04.scene: Two things lie before you. One is the photographs Cooper has brought. This morning’s British editorials are skeptical of the American case, and Bertrand Russell’s Committee of 100 will gather again in Grosvenor Square tonight. The American embassy wants to show the photographs to the press at an off-the-record background briefing at 5 p.m., and the BBC wants to run them on the evening news. Since morning de Zulueta has been telling Cooper that the government can hardly back the Americans firmly unless Parliament and the public believe the threat is real. The other is the Opposition. Gaitskell still suspects the President of dressing up antiaircraft missiles as offensive weapons, and he weighs the Soviet missiles on the same scale as the American missiles in Turkey. On your advice, Cooper can show the photographs to Gaitskell and Brown at 6 o’clock this evening at the house of the American minister, Roosevelt. And on your desk lies Ormsby-Gore’s cable No. 2650: the President has no military objection to trading away the bases in Turkey, words the President himself must never learn were passed on.

voices.text: He said that the bases in Turkey and other IRBM bases had become practically obsolete. He did not know whether a deal on the mutual closing of bases was possible, but from the military point of view he clearly saw no objection to it. You will understand how important it is that none of this should become known to any American, including the President himself.

The photographs must go out. We cannot stand with the Americans in the Commons over a threat the newspapers don’t believe in. Show them to Gaitskell too. He brings up Turkey because he doesn’t know. If he still brings it up once he knows, that is his responsibility.

Washington won’t be pleased to see the photographs released. They give away what our reconnaissance can do. But if the London papers and the BBC don’t believe us, we lose more. We’ll put them out with the location markings removed. If you wish, Prime Minister, we’ll brief the Opposition this evening.

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party)
voices.text: I hear you were angry at not being told first, Prime Minister. So am I. If a nuclear base in Cuba is grounds for attack, why not a nuclear base in Turkey? If you show me the photographs, I will look at them. But the question stands.

choices.text: On the strength of No. 2650, have the Foreign Office quietly work out the terms of a trade for the Turkish bases, and hold back the photographs
choices.why: If the next step is a deal, Britain should be the one already holding a plan
choices.after: The Foreign Office’s Western Department worked through the night on a paper: in what framework the 15 Jupiters in Turkey, Britain’s 60 Thors and Italy’s 30 Jupiters might be traded for the missiles in Cuba. When Lord Home brought it in the next morning, he did not look happy. The photographs were not shown on the BBC that night, and the newspapers’ skepticism lasted another day.

choices.text: Agree that the American embassy may release the photographs, location markings removed, to the press and the BBC, and have them shown to Gaitskell and Brown this evening
choices.why: The government can stand with America only if the public believes the threat
choices.after: The BBC and ITV ran the photographs in the evening, followed by Lord Home’s speech. Cooper recorded that Gaitskell, shown them at Roosevelt’s house, was visibly shaken. He admitted his suspicions had been wrong but would not let go of the comparison with Turkey. Late that night 2,000 people gathered in Grosvenor Square, and 300 police guarded the embassy’s glass doors. Washington complained that the photographs had been released first in London.

choices.text: Have RAF photo interpreters check the photographs, then let the government release them itself; brief the Opposition only once the statement has been made in the Commons
choices.why: American evidence should be confirmed by British eyes before it goes before the public
choices.after: Air Ministry interpreters received the photographs in the afternoon and studied them through the night. They reached the same conclusion. When the government released the photographs on the morning of the 24th, the newspapers came round a day late, and Gaitskell entered the Commons on the 25th without having been briefed. His first question was whether there had been any consultation.

note.text: Of the British Cabinet conclusions CC(62)61 (23 October), only the National Archives catalog entry has been checked, not the text. The photographs were released, with location markings removed, at the American embassy’s press briefing (5 p.m., 23 October), and Cooper described how it came about in a separate annex to his report. That Gaitskell was “visibly shaken” and that the Prime Minister was “annoyed” at the lack of advance notice both come from Cooper’s record. The Foreign Office study in choice A is hypothetical, built on the option under consideration at the time (the “base exchange” framework Ormsby-Gore passed to Bundy).

pressure.title: A Cable Even the President Knows Nothing About
pressure.text: Ormsby-Gore’s cable No. 2650 came with a warning that not even the President himself must learn of it. This is how words the ambassador heard in private inside the White House reach you. It is an asset no other allied head of government has, and the way to keep it is not to use it. Meanwhile Gaitskell will weigh the American missiles in Turkey on the same scale and ask whether the government was consulted in advance, and you have not hidden from Cooper your annoyance at being given no advance notice. For a prime minister whose standing in his own party has been shaky since the July reshuffle, being seen as America’s messenger would be the most damaging charge in the Commons. Releasing the photographs and showing them to the Opposition is a way of persuading the public and the House, but it also means putting American material out under the British government’s name.

HM-05.time: Noon (7 a.m. in Washington, 3 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-05.place: The Prime Minister’s study, Admiralty House
HM-05.title: The Political Track

map.caption: The quarantine line ran 500 nautical miles from Cape Maisí and took effect at 3 p.m. London time on 24 October.

HM-05.clock: 3 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (3 p.m. London), 23 hours until the statement in the Commons

telegram.from: de Zulueta (the Prime Minister’s private secretary)
telegram.subject: Classified material for use in the Commons statement of 25 October
telegram.text: Ambassador Bruce has checked with Washington. Cleared for release by US: at least 8 ballistic missile sites identified. Normally 4 launchers per site, 2 missiles per launcher. At least 30 missiles already on island. MRBM range over 1,000 miles; IRBM range 2,200 nautical miles. Over 20 Il-28 bombers identified. At least 5,000 Soviet military technicians. / Not to be used: exact location of photographs, means of reconnaissance, any judgment on presence of warheads. / US side has broadly accepted Prime Minister’s draft; its suggested amendments incorporated in text.

HM-05.event: Crossing point ⑤. At 3 p.m. London time (10 a.m. in Washington) the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) takes effect. At the same hour in New York, Acting Secretary-General U Thant sends Khrushchev and Kennedy an appeal in identical terms: for 2–3 weeks the Soviet Union should voluntarily suspend arms shipments and the United States the quarantine, and the two should negotiate. At its morning meeting Washington confirmed that Soviet ships had stopped or turned around, but the quiet day only made it more uneasy. In Havana Castro deployed 50 antiaircraft batteries. Khrushchev was writing Kennedy a letter calling the quarantine “piracy.”
HM-05.scene: Ambassador Bruce came at noon. You needed to ask what you could say in the Commons tomorrow and how much of it was classified, and he checked with Washington at once. But the question on your mind is not the speech. It is the one Ormsby-Gore put to Bundy: what is the next step on the political track? Short of war, there will have to be a conference at some point, and who should propose it? America, the Secretary-General, or Britain? If the framework is an exchange of bases, you and Lord Home see it as “a rather cynical exchange, and a weak ending to what America started.” A disarmament framework would be better: Kennedy and Khrushchev would call a conference to agree on the first stage of general disarmament, and before it there might be a “standstill” that halts arms shipments and lifts the blockade together. Ormsby-Gore is against both: the two camps are too far apart, there is no place for France, and America cannot lift the blockade without progress on removing the missiles. You speak to the President again at midnight tonight. Before then you must decide what Britain will bring to the call.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (ambassador in Washington, the Prime Minister’s thinking as passed to Bundy)
voices.text: The Prime Minister’s interest is in the next step on the political track. At some point there will have to be a conference. Who would it help to have propose it? The Prime Minister and Lord Home both think poorly of a base-exchange framework; it would look like a cynical trade and a weak ending to what America started. Speaking for myself, I hope you will tell the President plainly that I think neither calling a disarmament conference nor a standstill that includes lifting the blockade is a good idea.

Prime Minister, you must settle in advance what you will say in the Commons tomorrow. If Britain is first to propose a conference, Khrushchev will read it as a crack in the alliance, and Washington as a stab in the back. The Acting Secretary-General’s appeal came out today. Using it as an instrument is better than Britain stepping out in front.

Washington has broadly accepted your draft statement, Prime Minister. You can use the figures as they stand. But please leave out the locations and the means of reconnaissance. The President will brief you on the situation in tonight’s call. There was word this morning that the Soviet ships seem to have stopped.

choices.text: In tonight’s call, formally propose a Kennedy–Khrushchev disarmament conference, with a “standstill” halting arms shipments and lifting the blockade as its precondition
choices.why: Only by setting the missiles inside the larger frame of disarmament can a Cuba-for-Berlin bargain be headed off
choices.after: In the midnight call the President heard you out. Then he answered as Bundy had written it for him: the blockade could not be lifted without progress on removing the missiles. You said you would put it to him again in writing, and the next day the Foreign Office polished the paper. The Commons statement had to be rewritten to match it.

choices.text: Let it be known that Britain could host a conference in London, and pass the same message to Khrushchev through the Soviet ambassador, Soldatov
choices.why: The belief, held since 1959, that only Britain can build a bridge between America and the Soviet Union
choices.after: The President’s answer was short: this was no time to talk of a conference. Ambassador Soldatov came to the Foreign Office that night and said he would report to Moscow. The next morning Radio Moscow mentioned the British prime minister’s “constructive attitude,” and in Washington the people who had heard the broadcast called in Ormsby-Gore.

choices.text: Hold back from any British proposal of your own; tell the Commons you will use the Acting Secretary-General’s appeal as an “instrument,” and in the call simply hear how things stand
choices.why: Showing no crack in the alliance will press Khrushchev harder than any proposal
choices.after: In the midnight call you put forward no proposal, and the President told you the Soviet ships had stopped and that the first interception would come tomorrow. That night Cooper and de Zulueta gave the draft statement its final polish.

note.text: No record of the Kennedy–Macmillan call on the night of 24 October appears in FRUS or the Kennedy Library catalog. Bundy’s memo written before the call (Supp d385) sets out the Prime Minister’s thinking as Ormsby-Gore passed it on, and Macmillan’s memoir At the End of the Day describes the call. The memorandum on classified material for the statement recasts in memorandum form the “paragraphs from the Prime Minister’s draft statement” recorded in Bruce’s diary; no original document has been found. Choices A and B are the options Bundy’s memo records as what “the Prime Minister is thinking.”

HM-06.time: 11 a.m. (6 a.m. in Washington, 2 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-06.place: The Chamber of the House of Commons, Westminster
HM-06.title: Keeping the Way Back Open
HM-06.clock: 10 hours until the Security Council resumes (9 p.m. London)
HM-06.event: Crossing point ⑥. At 7 a.m. (Washington) the Soviet tanker Bucharest passed the quarantine line without being searched. Overnight Khrushchev’s letter reached Washington: the quarantine was piracy, Soviet ships would not stop, and if they were stopped there were means of response. That same day in Moscow the Presidium discussed for the first time trading the withdrawal of the missiles for a guarantee against invasion, but no one outside knows it. In New York U Thant issued his second appeal (Soviet ships should keep away from the quarantine line, and the United States should avoid a confrontation). On your desk is a report that came in last night: some Soviet ships seem to have changed course, though this is not yet confirmed.
HM-06.scene: Question Time ends and the Speaker calls you. You begin with the President’s message of Monday and Ambassador Bruce’s briefing: at least 30 missiles, with a range of more than 1,000 miles, enough to reach Washington and the Panama Canal; the TASS statement of 11 September and Gromyko’s assurance of 18 October were false; the President’s action was “carefully restrained.” You describe U Thant’s proposal for a 2–3 week standstill and close by saying that Britain hopes to move from easing tension toward wider negotiation, but cannot rely on words and promises: Soviet undertakings must be independently verified. Gaitskell rises. If a nuclear base in Cuba justifies an attack, would that not justify a Soviet attack on Turkey too? Was the British government consulted in advance? Has a meeting between Kennedy and Khrushchev been proposed? Shinwell asks: if there is a summit, will Britain be in it? Will British ships be searched? Selwyn Lloyd and Gardner ask about disarmament. You are at the dispatch box, and the House is watching to see whether you will bring out a British proposal of your own. You hold two cables that came yesterday: Ormsby-Gore’s, on the bases in Turkey, and Khrushchev’s reply to Bertrand Russell.

voices.text: In a matter of this gravity we cannot rely on mere words and promises. They must be independently checked and verified if confidence is to be restored.
voices.src: Hansard HC Deb 25 Oct 1962 vol 664 cc1053–64

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party)
voices.text: If the President clearly means to have the nuclear bases in Cuba removed, it can only be done by agreement or by attack. Should not every effort then be made to reach agreement? If the United States attacks Cuba on these grounds, how are we to stop the Soviet Union attacking Turkey in exactly the same way? And was the British government consulted before the decision to blockade?

It is reported that Khrushchev has proposed a summit to the President. Would a British representative take part in such a meeting, or is Britain to be left out of any consideration? And if the Soviet ships turn back, will the Americans go on searching British ships?

I think there are two considerations. First, that there should be no break or weakening in the alliance, which is perhaps the main purpose of this Soviet move. Secondly, that no avenue of retreat which may be open should be closed.
voices.src: Hansard HC Deb 25 Oct 1962 vol 664 cc1053–64

choices.text: Say the talk of a summit was only a reply to Bertrand Russell, that Britain will not be left out, and that it stands ready to host a conference in London
choices.why: A US–Soviet meeting without Britain would be the worst outcome for Britain
choices.after: The House cheered, and the front pages wrote of a “London summit.” In the evening a cable came from Ormsby-Gore: the White House called the Prime Minister’s remarks “premature,” and Rusk said Britain had given Khrushchev a stage instead of a way out. Radio Moscow praised the British prime minister’s “realism.”

choices.text: Say the alliance must not waver and no avenue of retreat be closed, and answer that, rather than a British proposal of your own, you will use the Acting Secretary-General’s approach as an instrument
choices.why: The principle that proposals are not made just “to be seen to be doing something”
choices.after: Gaitskell replied that leaving it to the United Nations would command wide support, and asked nothing more. You told Shinwell that British shipowners had agreed some weeks ago not to carry arms, so the question of searches would not arise. The full text of the statement went to Washington that afternoon. At 11:30 that night, on the telephone, the President’s first question was how the debate had gone.

choices.text: Tell Shinwell that British ships will submit to no search, and that Britain supports the resolution but reserves judgment on whether the quarantine is lawful
choices.why: Freedom of the seas is a principle Britain has upheld for 300 years
choices.after: The Chamber fell silent, then erupted. There was applause from the Opposition back benches, and the Conservative members behind you looked at one another. That night Ambassador Bruce came to say he was worried how the President would read your answer. You replied that it was a question of law, knowing it would not sound like a question of law alone.

note.text: The full statement is in Hansard. The House sat on the morning of 25 October because the session ended that day (prorogation); a new session opened with the Queen’s Speech on 30 October (Hansard, 25 October, “PROROGATION: HER MAJESTY’S SPEECH”). The figures in the statement (at least 30 missiles, more than 20 Il-28s, 5,000 technicians) were what the Americans had cleared for release, and Cooper kept updating them right up to the statement. Khrushchev’s reply to Bertrand Russell of 24 October said in substance that a summit would be useful; it was not a proposal between governments. Macmillan himself told the Commons on the 25th that Khrushchev had “only said, in his reply to Lord Russell’s telegram, that a summit would be useful; there was no proposal.”
note.src: Hansard HC Deb 25 Oct 1962 vol 664 cc1053–64; Supp d409; Supp d353(10/24)

HM-07.time: 11:30 p.m. (6:30 p.m. in Washington, 2:30 a.m. on the 26th in Moscow)
HM-07.title: Two Stages
HM-07.clock: About 10 hours until the first boarding (morning of the 26th, Washington)

telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.cc: Sent from the White House over the private line
telegram.at: Sent from Moscow 24 October 1962, received in London night of 25 October
telegram.subject: On the American naval quarantine
telegram.text: In substance: measures you have proclaimed an act of aggression violating sovereignty of Cuba and Soviet Union; stopping and searching ships on high seas no different from piracy / In substance: captains of Soviet ships will not obey orders of US Navy; Soviet Union has means to take steps needed to defend its rights / Asks how United States would react if Soviet Union did off American coast what President means to do over Cuba

HM-07.event: Crossing point ⑥. At 7 a.m. London time (2 a.m. in Washington) Khrushchev’s letter reached the White House. At the 10 a.m. meeting in Washington it was confirmed that 14 Soviet ships had turned back, and the tanker Bucharest had been let through. Tomorrow the East German passenger ship Völkerfreundschaft (1,500 passengers), which had called at Leningrad, reaches the quarantine line. McNamara opposed stopping the liner, and Robert Kennedy went so far as to say it would be better to remove the missiles by air strike than to stop Soviet ships on the high seas. In the afternoon the President sent a reply accepting U Thant’s second appeal. At 9 p.m. (London) the Security Council resumed, and Stevenson confronted Zorin with the photographs.
HM-07.scene: The President asks first: how did the debate go? You answer that it went very well, and that the point he gave you about the statement of 11 September went down especially well. The President runs through the numbers: 14 ships turned back, one tanker let through, an East German liner tomorrow, U Thant’s second appeal accepted, and last night Khrushchev’s “piracy” letter. Two tracks are running together, he says: one is the ships Khrushchev keeps sending, the other is U Thant’s effort to get the Soviet ships stopped. He does not want to sink any ships, but by tomorrow evening he will have to board and search one of them; after that, since work on the sites is going on, he will say that unless it stops he will widen the blockade and consider other action. Static breaks into the line, and you ask him once to repeat himself. You say the American reply to U Thant is very skillful and calm, and ask whether he will take up the question of the weapons inside Cuba with U Thant. Tonight the President wants your agreement.

voices.text: We think 14 ships have turned back today, probably the ones carrying offensive cargo. We stopped one tanker, asked where it was going, and it said from the Black Sea to Cuba, cargo petroleum. It was clearly a tanker, so we let it through.
We can’t let the principle be established that Khrushchev decides which ships go through.
I quite understand. I think you must do that. It seems to me there are two stages. The first is the question of the ships, and then comes the question of the weapons actually in Cuba.

voices.who: Lord Home (foreign secretary, advice before the call)
voices.text: Prime Minister, stopping a passenger liner is another matter. A ship with 1,500 passengers halted on the high seas will be in every newspaper in the world. But it would be better for Ormsby-Gore to say that to the President at the White House. On the telephone, give him your support and nothing more.

choices.text: Urge him to let the liner pass, accept U Thant’s first proposal (a 2–3 week standstill) and move into negotiation: the battle over the ships is already won
choices.why: The battle over the ships is won, so there is no need to push further
choices.after: The President said he could not accept the first proposal because it included lifting the blockade: lifting it while work on the sites went on would only buy Khrushchev time. You said you would put it to him again in writing, and the next day the Foreign Office drew up the paper. That paper became Britain’s formal proposal.

choices.text: Answer that you quite understand and he must do it. Sort it into two stages, the ships and then the weapons inside Cuba, and agree to speak again tomorrow night
choices.why: An ally’s support has to be put into words at the moment the other man is loneliest
choices.after: The President said he would call again at the same hour tomorrow night and would send you a copy of Khrushchev’s letter. You said you would very much like to see it. The next morning the Lebanese-flagged Marucla was boarded and searched, and the East German liner went through without inspection. That was how the battle over the ships began to wind down.

choices.text: Urge him, now that the ships have turned back, to extend the blockade to petroleum and add to the pressure: the moment the Soviets retreat is the moment to add cards
choices.why: The memory of the 1930s: stop when the other side backs off, and he reads it as weakness
choices.after: The President replied that an oil embargo would give the Soviets a pretext to do the same to him at Berlin, but that if work went on he would raise it from Saturday. The next day the White House signaled an embargo on jet fuel. No one ever told you how much your advice had gone into that decision.

note.text: The American record of this call is a verbatim transcript (FRUS XI d74), with passages lost to static marked “… garble ….” Khrushchev’s letter of 24 October (FRUS XI d61) likened the quarantine to piracy; the “copy of the letter” in this scene renders, in the form it would have taken on arrival in London, the copy the President offered in the call to send. The East German liner passed without inspection on 26 October, and that morning the Marucla (Lebanese-flagged, under Soviet charter) became the first ship to be boarded.

HM-08.time: Night (evening in Washington, early hours of the 27th in Moscow)
HM-08.title: Sixty Thor Missiles

map.caption: The 60 Thors in eastern England, the 30 Jupiters at Gioia del Colle in Italy and the 15 Jupiters near Izmir in Turkey were America’s intermediate-range missiles in Europe.

HM-08.clock: The deadline the President named in this call: 48 hours, to the night of the 28th

telegram.from: Telephone call, President Kennedy–Prime Minister Macmillan (Kennedy Library transcript)
telegram.subject: The UN route, a guarantee for Cuba, the Thor missiles
telegram.text: President: Ambassador Stevenson saw U Thant this afternoon and put forward a plan leading to a halt in arms shipments, a halt in work on the bases, and ultimately their dismantling. There is talk from the Soviet side that they might withdraw the weapons in return for a territorial guarantee for Cuba, but it is unofficial and can’t be relied on. If no political proposal for dismantling the bases comes within 48 hours, we will have to decide what to do about this buildup. / Prime Minister: One idea that has just occurred to me is to make Cuba like Belgium was: an international guarantee, with everyone guaranteeing its neutrality and inviolability. Is that possible? / Prime Minister: Another is for U Thant himself to propose to the UN that he take a team of experts and make sure the missiles are kept inoperable while a conference goes on. / Prime Minister: A third thing has occurred to me. If we want to help the Russians save face, would it be worth our while to undertake that our Thor missiles in England be immobilized for the same period, during the conference? / President: Let me put that into the machinery and I’ll be in touch with you. I don’t want too much dismantling, but that proposal might help. They may ask for Turkey and Italy too.

HM-08.event: Crossing point ⑦. In the morning the Marucla is boarded and searched. At 1:30 p.m. (Washington) ABC correspondent Scali heard from Fomin (Feklisov) of the Soviet embassy: “dismantling under UN supervision, an American pledge not to invade.” Between 6 and 9 p.m. Khrushchev’s long letter came into the State Department, asking that the two of them untie the knot of war together and saying a pledge not to invade would change the situation. At the same hour in Havana, in the basement of the Soviet embassy, Castro was writing a letter to Khrushchev, and in the Caribbean Soviet submarines were being hunted by American carrier groups. From the afternoon London had the sense that the question of the ships had gone and only the question of the bases remained. Work on the sites went on day and night.
HM-08.scene: In this call you do more of the talking than in any other. The President speaks of 48 hours and says there is talk from the Soviet side of trading withdrawal for a guarantee of Cuba. You bring up three ideas. Make Cuba, like Belgium in 1839, a country whose neutrality and inviolability everyone guarantees. Have U Thant lead a team of experts there himself to make sure the missiles stay inoperable while a conference sits. And third, if it would help the Russians save face, undertake to keep Britain’s Thor missiles inoperable for the same period. The President says he will have his people look into it, and adds that the Soviets may ask for Turkey and Italy as well. You say that at this stage any American move may affect Berlin, and he replies that this is why he has not done more. At the end of the call he asks about keeping General Norstad on, and says he will not call tomorrow but will be sure to speak to you before anything drastic. When you put down the receiver, Lord Home asks whether you mean to leave the Thor offer as a private remark or make it a proposal of the British government. The 60 missiles are with 20 RAF squadrons, and one of the keys is American.

voices.who: Harold Macmillan (by telephone, Kennedy Library transcript)
voices.text: One idea that has just occurred to me is to make Cuba like Belgium was: an international guarantee of an inviolable state, everyone guaranteeing its neutrality and inviolability independently.

voices.who: Harold Macmillan (by telephone, Kennedy Library transcript)
voices.text: If we want to help the Russians save face, would it be worth our while to undertake that our Thor missiles in England should be immobilized during the same period, during the conference?
voices.src: cmc/oct26/doc5; FRUS XI d87 mistranscribes this passage as “keep open eyes on all exiles”

voices.text: Let me put that into the machinery and I will be in touch with you on that.

Prime Minister, the Thors are under a dual key. Britain cannot promise on its own to make them inoperable. And if it is made public, Turkey and Italy will at once ask whether they are next, and Adenauer will ask whether the American bases in West Germany come after that. It is right to keep it a private remark. The President said he would have it looked into; wait for his answer.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (ambassador in Washington, advice by cable)
voices.text: In Washington the word “trade” is still taboo. Rusk and Bundy fear that the moment bases in Europe are bargained over, NATO will crack. But the President himself is different. Remember what I heard on the 23rd. What you have quietly put away may be put to use within days, Prime Minister.

choices.text: Leave the three ideas as private remarks and wait for the President’s people to answer. In writing, send only the U Thant route and the Belgian-style guarantee
choices.why: Publishing a British concession before America is ready to take it would produce not a deal but a rift
choices.after: No answer came from Washington. The next morning, when Radio Moscow publicly proposed a trade for the missiles in Turkey, what you had said the night before took on a different meaning.

choices.text: Tomorrow morning, through the BBC and the party leaders in the Commons, put forward a Thor freeze as a public proposal of the British government, and propose bringing Turkey and Italy into the same framework
choices.why: If Britain is first to open a face-saving way out, Khrushchev may be able to back down
choices.after: Lord Home argued against it all night, but at 7 a.m. you signed the draft of a statement for the BBC. Two hours after it went out, Radio Moscow read Khrushchev’s letter: he would take the missiles out of Cuba if the missiles in Turkey were taken out. The whole world read the two proposals side by side, and Washington asked whether Britain had arranged it with the Soviets beforehand.

choices.text: Contact de Gaulle and Adenauer tonight and first set up a joint three-power position that Europe’s missiles are not for bargaining. Withdraw the Thor offer
choices.why: Once the bargaining starts, Europe must speak with one voice so that America cannot sell Europe out
choices.after: Ambassador Dixon in Paris and Ambassador Steel in Bonn were woken in the night. Adenauer agreed at once. De Gaulle’s answer came in the morning: France would act with America but would not sign a joint declaration. De Gaulle had already told Acheson that he had been informed but not consulted, and he repeated it to Britain.

note.text: There are two transcripts of this call. FRUS XI d87 renders the Thor passage as “keep open eyes on all exiles which are here in England,” while the Kennedy Library microsite transcript (the same as the version in Macmillan’s memoirs) reads “immobilize our Thor missiles.” From 1959 to 1963, 60 Thor missiles were deployed with 20 RAF squadrons and operated under a dual-key system. On 1 August 1962 the minister of defense, Thorneycroft, told the Commons that the Thor deployment would end during 1963, and the last squadron was disbanded in August 1963. How the Americans examined the proposal has not been established (Phase 1, unconfirmed item 7).
note.src: FRUS XI d87; cmc/oct26/doc5; Phase 1 issue 15

pressure.title: Sixty on British Soil
pressure.text: The 60 Thor missiles are with 20 RAF squadrons, and one of the keys is American. Offering to keep them inoperable during a conference puts the one thing you own on the bargaining table, and the President answered only that he would have his people look into it. The Thor is a missile whose withdrawal during next year was announced in the Commons last August, and word comes through Ormsby-Gore that Skybolt, the next pillar of Britain’s nuclear force, is wavering in Washington too. Britain has little to offer, and some read that as the reason you were first to bring up frameworks such as a Belgian-style guarantee or U Thant’s inspection on the spot. The President answered that any American move could affect Berlin, and those words point straight at what you have feared most since the night of 22 October. Make public the offer you kept private and it becomes Britain’s proposal; withdraw it and you go back to being the one who listens.

HM-09.time: Saturday, 3 p.m. (10 a.m. in Washington, 5 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-09.place: Admiralty House, a meeting of senior ministers
HM-09.title: Black Saturday in London
HM-09.clock: About 32 hours until the President’s 48 hours run out (night of the 28th)

telegram.kind: Radio text (Moscow broadcast, Foreign Office monitoring summary)
telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.cc: Foreign Office Soviet desk, Prime Minister’s Office
telegram.at: 5 p.m., 27 October 1962 (Moscow); monitored in London 3 p.m.
telegram.subject: Missiles in Cuba and Turkey
telegram.text: In substance: you are uneasy that Cuba lies 90 miles from US coast, but Turkey borders Soviet Union and US missiles stand there / Proposal: USSR willing to remove from Cuba means regarded as offensive; US to remove like means from Turkey / In substance: both to guarantee this within Security Council framework; USSR to pledge not to invade Turkey, US not to invade Cuba / Proposal: carried out within 2–3 weeks, verified on site by UN representatives

HM-09.event: Crossing point ⑧. At 5 p.m. Moscow time (3 p.m. in London, 10 a.m. in Washington) Radio Moscow read out Khrushchev’s second letter. Its terms differ from yesterday’s letter: a trade with Turkey. The White House spokesman issued a public rejection at noon (Washington). That same day a U-2 was shot down over Cuba by a Soviet surface-to-air missile, killing Major Anderson (4:20 p.m. London), and a U-2 from Alaska lost its way and strayed into Soviet airspace. In the Caribbean American destroyers were dropping practice depth charges on the Soviet submarine B-59. In London none of this is known yet. What you know is the radio, and the 48 hours the President spoke of in last night’s call.
HM-09.scene: On Saturday afternoon you have called in a few senior ministers, Lord Home among them. On the face of it the Radio Moscow proposal is plausible. It follows the same logic as the comparison with Turkey that Gaitskell made in the Commons on Thursday, and it is one step from the Thor freeze you raised on the private line last night. But you are a man who remembers 1938. A deal that buys off one’s own danger at an ally’s expense: Britain called that Munich. Turkey is a NATO ally, and its government regards the Jupiters as a symbol of its own defense. In the evening word comes from Washington. The President has decided to deal with Khrushchev’s letters in chronological order and according to whether they are official: he will answer yesterday’s private letter and meet today’s public demand with the spokesman’s rejection. Lord Home says the time has come for Britain to stand publicly beside the President. The question is how: write to Khrushchev directly, make a statement to the Commons, or offer last night’s Thor idea as a bridge to a deal. The President has said he will not call today.

voices.who: Harold Macmillan (looking back, in the Commons, 30 October)
voices.text: The President decided to deal with the Russian letters in chronological order and according to whether or not they were official. The public demand for the sell-out of Turkey he answered only by a public rejection from the White House spokesman. That decision certainly had the support of Her Majesty’s Government. One cannot avoid one’s own dangers by a dishonorable deal at the expense of an ally.

Prime Minister, the private channel is no longer enough. We must say, with the world watching, where Britain stands. Write to Khrushchev: once the bases in Cuba are dealt with under UN control, the way opens to a test ban and disarmament. Open a way back for him, but don’t put a single word about Turkey in it.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (ambassador in Washington, report by telephone)
voices.text: Since Saturday morning the White House has been divided over Khrushchev’s two letters. Some say a Turkish trade is fair; Rusk and Bundy say NATO will fall apart. The President is moving toward answering yesterday’s letter. If you raise Turkey now, Prime Minister, you could tip the scales inside the White House. Which way they would tip, I can’t tell you.

voices.who: De Gaulle (Paris, as relayed by Ambassador Dixon)
voices.text: France did not oppose the blockade, and if America comes under pressure somewhere like Berlin, France will act with America. But France will not add a single word to a bargain that trades Europe’s bases for Cuba. Such a bargain would only show that America has no will to defend Europe.
voices.src: FRUS XI d46 (based on the gist of Acheson’s report of 10/22)

choices.text: Urge the President to accept the Turkish trade, and announce that Britain’s Thor freeze will go into the same framework. A deal today is better
choices.why: Avoiding nuclear war is the true meaning of an alliance, more than a few missiles
choices.after: Your message reached Washington at 7 p.m. Those inside the White House who thought the trade fair took the British prime minister’s message to the President. That night the Turkish ambassador called on Rusk to protest at Britain’s remarks. In Bonn Adenauer said just one sentence to reporters: who is next?

choices.text: Oppose the trade and, with your senior ministers’ agreement, send Khrushchev an open letter: once the Cuban bases are dealt with under UN control, the way to disarmament opens
choices.why: The principle you have held since 1938: leave the way back open, but close the road to selling out an ally
choices.after: You wrote the letter with Lord Home. You had read Khrushchev’s letter of yesterday and the President’s reply; once the offensive missile bases in Cuba were dealt with under effective UN control and the situation was normalized, the way would open to a more general agreement on armaments; early agreement on a test ban and guidance on the first stage of disarmament would be possible. It was decided to send the letter to the embassy in Moscow as an emergency cable at noon tomorrow. That night in Washington Robert Kennedy was meeting Dobrynin.

choices.text: Issue a public statement proposing an immediate Kennedy–Khrushchev–Macmillan summit, on condition that work on the sites stops and the blockade stays in place while it sits
choices.why: The belief that only when a third man enters a room with two in it does a deal become an agreement
choices.after: The statement went out on the evening BBC news. That night Khrushchev said through TASS that he would “study the British prime minister’s proposal carefully.” The President did not call. Instead Ormsby-Gore telephoned at 11 p.m. to say the White House had decided to make no comment on the British statement. The silence was the answer.

note.text: No Kennedy–Macmillan call of 27 October appears in FRUS or the Kennedy Library catalog, and in the call of the 26th Kennedy said he would not telephone the next day. The consultation with senior ministers and the decision to intervene publicly come from Macmillan’s speech in the Commons on 30 October (“some of my senior colleagues”). The names of those present are not confirmed in the record, so they are not given. The text of Khrushchev’s second letter is rendered in the form of a Foreign Office monitoring summary; the original is in FRUS VI. De Gaulle’s words are a gist adapted to this scene from what he told Acheson on 22 October (“France will act in accord with you”). British summer time ended in the early hours of 28 October, so until that day Britain was two hours behind Moscow.
note.src: Hansard HC Deb 30 Oct 1962; FRUS XI d46·d87; Phase 1 issues 11·12

pressure.title: A Man Who Remembers 1938
pressure.text: The second letter Radio Moscow read out is one step from the Thor freeze you raised on the private line last night, and it follows the same logic as Gaitskell’s comparison with Turkey in the Commons. That makes it all the more dangerous. In October 1938 you were among the few who would not vote for Chamberlain’s Munich agreement, and a deal that buys off one’s own danger at an ally’s expense is what Britain calls Munich. Turkey is a NATO ally that regards the Jupiters as a symbol of its own defense, and if Britain urges that deal, Ankara and Bonn will conclude that Britain too might be traded away. You later told the Commons that such a deal would have been a super-Munich. Where you stand this Saturday afternoon before your senior ministers is the first moment Britain stands publicly beside America, and the moment you answer your own 1938.

HM-10.time: Sunday, noon (7 a.m. in Washington, 3 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-10.place: Admiralty House, and the House of Commons on 30 October
HM-10.title: The Letter That Answered Itself
HM-10.clock: 2 hours 15 minutes until the Moscow broadcast (2:15 p.m. London)

telegram.kind: Letter (sent to the embassy in Moscow as an emergency cable)
telegram.to: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers
telegram.cc: Ambassador in Moscow (for immediate delivery); senior diplomat at the Soviet embassy in London (handed over 2:30 p.m.)
telegram.subject: Your letter of 27 October and the President’s reply
telegram.text: Dear Mr. Chairman, / I have had the opportunity of studying your letter of yesterday to President Kennedy and his reply. / The essence of the position reached so far is that, if the problem raised by the offensive missile bases in Cuba is dealt with under effective United Nations control and the situation in the area is normalized, the way will be open for us all to move toward a more general agreement on armaments. / We might, for instance, reach early agreement on a treaty banning nuclear tests, on which so much progress has already been made, and we might give firm guidance on the main elements of the first stage of disarmament. / I trust this may be the sign of a new determination to solve the problems that beset the world. / I therefore ask you to take the action needed to make all this possible. It is an opportunity which must not be missed.

HM-10.event: Crossing point ⑨. In Moscow the Presidium met at 10 a.m. (8 a.m. in London) at the Novo-Ogaryovo dacha. Dobrynin’s cable relayed what Robert Kennedy had said, and there was a report that an American attack was imminent. Khrushchev dictated a letter, and Radio Moscow was to read it at 5 p.m. (Moscow). In Britain summer time had ended in the early hours, so London was now three hours behind Moscow. At broadcast time it would be 9 a.m. in both Washington and Havana.
HM-10.scene: The cable went out at noon. At 2:30 p.m., the time it was expected to be delivered in Moscow, the letter was also handed to the senior diplomat at the Soviet embassy in London. The aim was to set the British government publicly and squarely beside the President. As you later told the Commons, after that there was nothing to do but wait and see what happened. Then, at 2:15 p.m., Khrushchev’s statement came, not through diplomatic channels but over the radio: the missiles would be crated and sent back to the Soviet Union under UN supervision. It was the very moment your letter was being delivered in Moscow. Two days later, on Tuesday, you must account for the week to the House in its new session. Shinwell will ask whether you have had a reply from Khrushchev, and a Labour backbencher will say the Prime Minister did nothing but say “yes” to the President, an office boy carrying messages. A Conservative backbencher will say Britain played its part as a “third force.” What remains is what you will tell the House, and what you will ask of the President.

voices.text: It would have been a sort of super-Munich, and might easily have led to the collapse of the defense of the free world.

I would ask anyone who has carried any responsibility, and I have carried some, whether he could help feeling relief when that message came over the radio at 2:15. And there was a special satisfaction that this time the relief could be enjoyed without shame.
Has the Prime Minister had a reply to his message to Khrushchev?
The letter answered itself, because he undertook to withdraw the missiles, which was the only thing we asked him to do.

It caused all of us great anxiety that the British government was not consulted before the decision. The decision the President took could have had the gravest consequences for Europe. It is not satisfactory that such a decision should be taken without the principal NATO governments concerned having any chance to give their views. Better arrangements for consultation must be made in future.

choices.text: Take up America’s failure to consult in advance openly in the Commons, and press the President for reform of NATO’s consultation arrangements and a British share in nuclear decisions
choices.why: In the next crisis, after the relief, Britain must not be a country that is merely informed
choices.after: Gaitskell applauded, and after hearing General Strong’s report on 19 November you grew warier of Washington. The report said America had been ready to go it alone without consulting its allies, and prepared, if a counterstroke came at Berlin, to see it run on to nuclear war. In December at Nassau you obtained Polaris in place of Skybolt. The consultation arrangements did not change.

choices.text: Pay tribute in the Commons to the President’s courage and say a “super-Munich” was avoided, but push the test ban treaty and the principle of verification as the next task
choices.why: The one gift the crisis left behind, the principle of verification, must be carried over into disarmament
choices.after: The speech was judged moderate yet firm. When General Strong reported on 19 November that America had been ready to go it alone, you and Lord Home put American “overconfidence” on the agenda for the next summit. At Nassau in December you got Polaris, and in August 1963 the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in Moscow: the very treaty you had written of in your letter of 28 October.

choices.text: Tell the Commons that Britain played its part in easing tension between the two sides, and ask the President to give Britain a seat at the next US–Soviet talks
choices.why: The British public must know what Britain did if Britain is to keep its seat in the next crisis
choices.after: Fell, the member for Yarmouth, said the Prime Minister had “shown the world the way,” while from the Labour back benches came the words “office boy.” There was no British seat at the Kuznetsov–McCloy negotiations in New York. In a call on 15 November the President told you he was pressing for the withdrawal of the Il-28 bombers, and the American record set down your words only as “the Prime Minister said.”

note.text: Macmillan read out the full text of the letter again in the Commons on 30 October. The time of the broadcast is in dispute. The “2:15” in the Commons speech is London time, while the FRUS footnote gives the broadcast as 5 p.m. Moscow time. Because British summer time ended in the early hours of 28 October, London was three hours behind Moscow that day, and 5 p.m. in Moscow was 2 p.m. in London. The 15 minutes may be the gap between the start of the broadcast and the time it was heard, but the Phase 1 report reached no conclusion. In the debate of 30 October the phrase “office boy” was used by the Labour member Fernyhough, and “third force” by Fell, Conservative member for Yarmouth. British summer time ended at 3 a.m. on 28 October 1962, so 17:00 in Moscow was 14:00 in London, and the “2:15” in the Commons speech can be read as the time it was heard after the broadcast began.
