HM-H1.time: 9 a.m. (4 a.m. in Washington, noon in Moscow)
HM-H1.place: Foreign Office, the foreign secretary’s room
HM-H1.title: A Framework for Standstill and Disarmament
HM-H1.clock: About 4 hours until the first boarding at the quarantine line (the Marucla, around 1 p.m. London time)

telegram.from: Foreign Office, Western Department and Disarmament Department
telegram.cc: Ambassador in Washington (to go over the private line)
telegram.subject: Framework for a political settlement of the Cuban crisis (British proposal)
telegram.text: 1. Standstill: Soviet Union to halt arms shipments to Cuba and work on bases; United States to suspend enforcement of quarantine. Duration 2–3 weeks. Observers of acting Secretary-General to verify both sides. / 2. Talks: within standstill period President Kennedy and Chairman Khrushchev to meet and agree guidelines for first stage of general disarmament. UK to take part as co-chairman of Eighteen-Nation Disarmament Conference, Geneva. / 3. Bases: question of medium-range missile bases on foreign territory to be handled as item in first stage of disarmament; direct exchange of Cuba for any particular base to be avoided. / 4. Guarantee: inviolability and neutrality of Cuba to be guaranteed by powers concerned (Belgian model).

HM-H1.event: Your proposal has gone to Washington in writing. It is the very plan that Ormsby-Gore himself, as Bundy recorded in a memo beforehand, had opposed. The President’s answer came a day later: the quarantine could not be lifted without progress on removing the missiles, and a standstill while construction went on would only buy Khrushchev time. That same morning the Marucla was boarded, and in New York Stevenson handed U Thant the American terms (no more arms shipments, a halt to construction, dismantling). Radio Moscow called the British proposal “constructive,” and that one word cost it its credit in Washington.
HM-H1.scene: In Lord Home’s room lies a paper drawn up by the Western and Disarmament Departments. It is the framework you wanted: Cuba placed not in a trade of bases but in the larger framework of disarmament, with Britain given a seat as co-chairman of the Geneva disarmament conference. But Washington’s answer was plain, and Ormsby-Gore reports Bundy as saying that if the Prime Minister pushes this, the President will start to see Britain not as an ally but as a mediator. Lord Home sets out three courses. Withdraw the plan and return to the President’s side on tonight’s call. Make it public in the Commons and at the UN, and put Britain’s weight behind U Thant’s 2–3-week standstill. Or send it first to Paris and Bonn and make it a common European position. The construction goes on, and in Washington it is not yet dawn.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (ambassador in Washington, passing on what Bundy told him)
voices.text: Bundy said I must make it clear to the Prime Minister that this is an unacceptable position. Without progress on removing the missiles, the United States cannot lift the blockade. I agree with him. The two camps are too far apart, and there is no room for France to come in.

Prime Minister, a plan that Moscow praises is a dead plan in Washington. If you want to keep it alive you must take it to the UN, and then Britain stands against America. Withdraw it, and Britain loses one plan, nothing more. I am for withdrawing.

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party, by telephone)
voices.text: Prime Minister, put the plan before the House. The Opposition will back it to the hilt. If Britain turns the acting secretary-general’s appeal into a resolution, even America will not veto an ally’s proposal.

choices.text: Make the plan public and table U Thant’s 2–3-week standstill as a British Security Council resolution, writing in a halt to construction as a condition to bring the Americans round
choices.why: The reckoning that America would not veto a resolution tabled by an ally
choices.after: The resolution went to the Security Council on 27 October. The Soviet Union backed it at once, and the United States did not use its veto. A three-week standstill began. U Thant’s observers reached Havana in early November, but Castro refused to let them inspect the bases, and the construction went on. The negotiations dragged on.

choices.text: Withdraw the plan and return to the President’s side on tonight’s call: keep the proposal as a private thought and speak only of the U Thant channel and a guarantee for Cuba
choices.why: The reckoning that losing one plan weighs less than losing your place as an ally
choices.after: On the night call you never mentioned the plan. Instead you spoke of a Belgian-style guarantee and on-the-spot verification by U Thant, and for the third time you raised the Thors. The President said he would have his staff look into it. The Foreign Office paper went into a file.

choices.text: Send the plan first to Paris and Bonn, make it a joint European proposal with de Gaulle and Adenauer, then put it to Washington again
choices.why: The reckoning that America can brush off Britain alone, but not three European powers
choices.after: Ambassadors Dixon and Steel took the paper in that night. Adenauer said he would agree if the item on bases came out. De Gaulle’s answer came in the morning: France would act with the United States but would not sign a joint paper. He had been informed but not consulted, he had told Acheson, and he told the British the same.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Bundy’s memo of 24 October records two ideas the Prime Minister had in mind (calling a Kennedy–Khrushchev disarmament summit, and a standstill pairing a halt to arms shipments with the lifting of the blockade) and notes that Ormsby-Gore himself opposed both. Macmillan never formally made this proposal, and in the Commons on 25 October he said Britain would refrain from proposals of its own. In 1962 Britain was the Western co-chairman of the Eighteen-Nation Disarmament Conference in Geneva. The memorandum is invented; there is no original.
note.src: Supp d385; Hansard 1962-10-25; Phase 1 ending logic E

HM-H2.time: 11 p.m. (6 p.m. in Washington, 1 a.m. on the 28th in Moscow)
HM-H2.title: The Third Chair
HM-H2.clock: About 24 hours until the President’s 48 hours run out (the night of the 28th)

telegram.at: Night, 27 October 1962 (early hours of the 28th in Moscow)
telegram.subject: Soviet response to the Prime Minister’s proposal for talks
telegram.text: Gromyko summoned me tonight. Soviet Government regard British Prime Minister’s proposal for three-power talks as “constructive”; Chairman can accept London as venue. / Conditions: US quarantine and Soviet arms shipments to be suspended for duration of talks. On halt to base construction in Cuba, said only that it “can be discussed.” Want agenda to cover not only Cuba but “foreign bases in Europe” and “normalization of the German question.” / My assessment: Moscow seeks to put Berlin on agenda as price for accepting talks at all. Precisely the bargain Prime Minister warned President against on 22 October.

HM-H2.event: You have publicly proposed a three-power summit. Within a day Moscow spoke of “considering” it, and tonight Gromyko has set out conditions. Washington has made no comment. You do not yet know all that happened in Washington today: Khrushchev’s second letter, the U-2 shot down, the U-2 over Alaska, the depth charges in the Caribbean. Nor do you know that at 7:45 p.m. (Washington time) Robert Kennedy met Dobrynin. What you know is Ormsby-Gore’s call tonight: the White House has decided not to comment on the British proposal, and the President will not telephone tonight.
HM-H2.scene: Ambassador Roberts’s cable hands back to you, word for word, what you wrote to the President on 22 October. If Khrushchev came to a conference, you wrote, he would try to trade Cuba for Berlin, and that must be avoided at all costs. Now you are the one who has proposed that conference. Lord Home says nothing. De Zulueta asks what you mean to do: accept Moscow’s conditions and hold the talks, press on with Berlin off the agenda as your condition, or withdraw the proposal and return to the President’s side. Withdraw, and the Commons and the papers will ask questions; press on, and Washington will see Britain as a mediator, which is to say, not as an ally. The private line is silent.

voices.text: Prime Minister, the White House has decided to say nothing about the British proposal today. That is the worst answer there is. The President will not telephone tonight. From what I hear, people inside the White House have begun calling Britain a “mediator.” You know better than I do that the word cannot sit beside the word “ally.”

Gromyko’s conditions are the very bargain you warned against on 22 October, Prime Minister. The moment Berlin goes on the agenda, Adenauer will never forgive Britain, and the Americans will not come. The conference becomes a room with only Britain and the Soviet Union left in it. It is not too late to withdraw.

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party, by telephone)
voices.text: Prime Minister, Moscow has accepted London. If the Americans do not come, that is their choice. In 1959, too, Britain went to Moscow alone. Miss this chance, and in the next crisis Britain will once again be a country that is merely informed.

choices.text: Press on with the conference: drop Berlin from the agenda in return for a halt to construction and UN observers, and ask U Thant to preside
choices.why: The belief that once talks open, construction and blockade both stop, and time comes over to the side of peace
choices.after: U Thant agreed to preside, and Moscow agreed to drop Berlin from the agenda. On 1 November the United States announced it would attend, since staying away would have been the greater rift. A three-week standstill began, and construction in Cuba went on all the while. The negotiations dragged on.

choices.text: Withdraw the proposal: at noon tomorrow send Khrushchev a letter that speaks only of dealing with the Cuban bases under UN control and of disarmament to follow, and stand by the President
choices.why: A return to your judgment of 22 October: a conference would raise Britain’s standing but could cost Berlin
choices.after: That night you wrote the letter with Lord Home. It contained not one word about a conference. The next morning’s papers wrote of “the Prime Minister’s retreat,” and Gaitskell will raise it on Monday. The cable went at noon, and at 2:15 p.m. the radio brought other news.

choices.text: Accept the talks on Moscow’s terms: put Berlin and foreign bases on the agenda, but make verification that the Cuban missiles are inoperable the first item
choices.why: The reckoning that only with everything on one table can no single issue become a cause of war
choices.after: The Americans did not come. In November the London conference became a meeting of Britain, the Soviet Union and U Thant, while the United States looked on with the quarantine still in place. The missiles in Cuba stayed “for the duration of the talks,” and the talks moved on to Berlin and dragged on. In the spring of 1963 the missiles were still there.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In the Commons on 25 October Macmillan said Britain would refrain from proposals of its own, and Khrushchev mentioned a summit only in his reply to Bertrand Russell. Gromyko’s conditions and Ambassador Roberts’s cable are invented, and the Soviet Presidium records contain no plan for a London conference. The premise of Ending F (the missiles stay) is taken from B46 ① and B61 ① in the Phase 1 ending logic.
note.src: Hansard 1962-10-25; NSA #812 Doc 7; Phase 1 ending logic E · F

HM-H3.time: Morning (dawn in Washington, midday in Moscow)
HM-H3.title: The Price of Distance
HM-H3.clock: A few hours until the first boarding at the quarantine line (the Marucla, around 1 p.m. London time)

telegram.at: Early hours, 26 October 1962 (night of the 25th in Washington)
telegram.subject: White House reaction to the British position
telegram.text: President sent for me last night and talked for nearly an hour. Called British Government’s attitude a “personal hurt” and referred to his relationship with the Prime Minister since their Bermuda meeting last December. / Rusk observed that remark refusing search of British ships is being quoted hourly by Soviet radio. Sir Patrick Dean’s abstention in Security Council has been lumped together with abstentions of Ghana and UAR. / Bundy said privately that “British attitude” will be taken into account in December review of Skybolt program. / My assessment: unless Britain publicly changes position within days, private line will stay open but go unused.

HM-H3.event: Three days have passed since Britain distanced itself from the quarantine. In New York the British representative, Sir Patrick Dean, abstained in the vote on the American resolution, and Radio Moscow quoted “British realism” every day. In the Commons Gaitskell praised the government’s “independent judgment,” and on the Conservative back benches discontent with your leadership has made itself heard for the first time. In Washington fourteen Soviet ships have turned back, U Thant’s second appeal has been accepted, and this morning the Marucla was picked as the first ship to be boarded. London had a part in none of it. The President did not telephone on the night of 25 October.
HM-H3.scene: Lord Home has spoken of resigning. A quiet man, he said it quietly: as foreign secretary he would take responsibility for what had become of relations with America. You talked him out of it, but his words remain. Britain had tried to be a bridge between the Soviet Union and America, but a bridge stands only when both banks will bear it. On your desk lies Ormsby-Gore’s cable, with its sentence that the private line will stay open but go unused. The papers are divided: the Guardian and the Daily Mirror write of the Prime Minister’s independence, The Times and the Telegraph of “a crisis in the alliance.” You are the man who turned his back on Chamberlain in 1938, and who, as Chancellor of the Exchequer at Suez in 1956, saw how America brought Britain to a halt. What you learned then was that no British foreign policy gets anywhere without America. If the President does not telephone tonight, you will have to make the call.

voices.text: Prime Minister, I do not believe Britain can stand in the middle. If 1956 taught us anything, it was that. Once America decides to go on without Britain, Britain is nowhere. Turn back now, and the wound remains, but so does the bridge. If you do not turn back, someone else will have to take my place.

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party)
voices.text: For the first time the government has acted on British judgment, not on orders from Washington. We support that. Now go one step further. Let Britain put forward a plan, with the acting secretary-general, to bring both sides to one table. Only Britain can do that.

Prime Minister, I speak not as an ambassador but as an old friend. In Monday’s letter the President wrote that he wanted you to be the first to know. Imagine what the man who wrote that sentence feels at this moment. It is not too late yet. But after Saturday it will be.

choices.text: Keep your distance, and publicly offer Britain as the mediator who, with the acting secretary-general, brings the Americans and the Soviets to one table
choices.why: The reckoning that a country that declares its independence and turns back three days later looks lightweight to both sides
choices.after: The proposal went out on the BBC that evening. Within a day Moscow spoke of “considering” it; Washington said nothing. Ormsby-Gore telephoned that night: the White House had decided not to comment on the British statement. That silence was the answer.

choices.text: Telephone the President yourself tonight, tell him the British government will issue a public statement of full support for the quarantine, and change Britain’s position in the Security Council
choices.why: The lesson of Suez in 1956: without America, no British policy stands
choices.after: The call began awkwardly and went on a long time. Only toward the end did the President fall back into his usual manner, explaining the talks between U Thant and Stevenson and the talk of guarantees on the Soviet side. In that call you put forward three proposals. Lord Home did not resign. The next day in the Commons Gaitskell used the words “office boy” for the first time.

choices.text: Keep your distance, and tell the Soviet ambassador that Britain will table U Thant’s first appeal (a 2–3-week standstill) as a resolution in the Security Council
choices.why: The reckoning that by putting on the UN stage a plan America cannot accept, Britain opens a way out for both sides
choices.after: The resolution went to the Security Council on 27 October, and the Soviet Union backed it at once. The United States could not use its veto: vetoing an ally’s proposal would have been the greater rift. A three-week standstill began, and construction in Cuba went on all the while.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Britain supported the American resolution in the Security Council (Sir Patrick Dean’s speech), and an agreement with British shipowners not to carry arms was already in place. The Skybolt air-to-surface missile program was in fact canceled by the United States in December 1962 and replaced with Polaris at the Nassau meeting; this scene brings that decision forward as a lever of pressure. The cable is invented; there is no original.
note.src: Hansard 1962-10-25; FRUS XI d87; Phase 1 ending logic E

HM-H4.time: 8 p.m. (3 p.m. in Washington, 10 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-H4.title: One of Two Keys
HM-H4.clock: About 27 hours until the President’s 48 hours run out (the night of the 28th)

telegram.subject: Reactions to the public proposal to freeze the Thors
telegram.text: President sent for me at noon. White House deeply embarrassed that Prime Minister’s Thor freeze proposal came out same morning as Turkish proposal in Moscow broadcast. Rusk said “Britain has handed Khrushchev the second key.” / President himself takes different view. Said there are those who think a Turkish trade fair, and that Prime Minister’s proposal had “widened that road.” He is weighing whether to put a framework covering European bases as a whole to ExComm tonight. / Turkish ambassador has protested to State Department; General Norstad reports unrest in NATO Council from Paris. / My assessment: if Prime Minister withdraws proposal tonight, President will take the road of answering yesterday’s letter. If not, White House scales may tip toward a trade.

HM-H4.event: At 7 a.m. your BBC statement went out: a proposal that Britain’s Thor missiles be kept inoperable for the duration of talks, and that Turkey and Italy could be brought into the same framework. Two hours later Radio Moscow read out Khrushchev’s second letter: he would remove the missiles from Cuba if the missiles in Turkey were removed. The whole world read the two proposals side by side. In Washington the White House press secretary issued a public rejection at noon, but it made no mention of the British proposal. In the afternoon (Washington time) word came that a U-2 had been shot down over Cuba. The White House went into its evening meeting with Khrushchev’s two letters and the British proposal on the same desk.
HM-H4.scene: The day has been read two ways. Moscow speaks of British “realism,” Ankara of British “betrayal,” and Bonn asks “who is next?” Several Conservative MPs have written to you, and Gaitskell has praised the Prime Minister for the first time. Ormsby-Gore’s cable says the President stands between two roads: answering yesterday’s private letter, or moving to a framework that deals with all the European bases at once. Your proposal has widened the second road. Lord Home has said nothing since this morning. One of the two keys to each Thor is American, so by promising on its own to make them inoperable, Britain has in effect turned the American key for it. Tonight you have three courses. Press on and urge the President to accept the Turkish trade. Withdraw and stand by the President as he answers yesterday’s letter. Or detach Britain’s Thors alone and hand them over to the U Thant channel.

voices.text: The President said there are those who think a Turkish trade fair, and that the Prime Minister’s proposal had widened that road. Rusk said Britain had handed Khrushchev the second key. Whichever way you go tonight, Prime Minister, the scales in the White House will move.

Prime Minister, I was against it last night and I was against it this morning. But the words are out. The question now is how far Britain carries them. Carry them as far as Turkey, and Britain is trading away an ally’s security over its head. It would be doing to Turkey what Britain did to Czechoslovakia in 1938.

voices.who: Hugh Gaitskell (leader of the Labour Party, by telephone)
voices.text: Prime Minister, this morning’s statement was right. The missiles in Turkey and the missiles in Cuba sit on the same scales, and the world knows it. Push the President to accept. Tonight you are the one man who can stop the world ending over a handful of missiles.

choices.text: Press on: urge that Khrushchev’s offer be accepted within a framework that keeps the Turkish, Italian and British missiles inoperable together under UN supervision
choices.why: The reckoning that avoiding nuclear war, more than a handful of missiles, is what an alliance is truly for
choices.after: At the night meeting the President took the second road. On the morning of 28 October the White House made public a plan to withdraw the intermediate-range missiles from Turkey, Italy and Britain together with those in Cuba, under UN supervision, and Moscow accepted it that day. The crisis was over. Ankara and Bonn remembered that day differently.

choices.text: Withdraw the proposal: narrow the Thor offer to “an assumption for when talks open,” and at noon tomorrow send Khrushchev a letter that speaks only of the Cuban bases
choices.why: The memory of 1938: a deal that buys your own safety at an ally’s expense is Munich
choices.after: The statement went out at 10 p.m. The papers wrote of “the Prime Minister’s one-day retreat.” The President took the road of answering yesterday’s letter, and that night Robert Kennedy met Dobrynin. At noon the next day your letter went to Moscow, and at 2:15 p.m. the radio gave the answer. Turkey was mentioned nowhere.

choices.text: Leave Turkey out and hand only Britain’s Thors to the U Thant channel: a plan for UN observers to verify the Cuban and British missiles as inoperable over the same period
choices.why: The reckoning that offering only what is Britain’s own lets the other side save face without selling out an ally
choices.after: U Thant took up the plan and sent it to both sides. Moscow said Britain alone was not enough and brought up Turkey again, and the White House, using the British plan as a stepping stone, put Turkey into a public framework rather than a private one. On 28 October the trade was made in public. Britain’s Thors were due to be withdrawn in 1963 anyway; Turkey’s Jupiters were not.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Macmillan’s proposal to freeze the Thors came up only privately, in the call of 26 October, and no record of any follow-up study on the American side has been found (Phase 1 unconfirmed item 7). On 1 August 1962 the British government announced in the Commons that the Thors would be withdrawn during 1963, and the last squadron was disbanded in August 1963. In reality the Turkish Jupiters were withdrawn in April 1963 under a secret understanding. The premise of Ending D is taken from B65 (acceptance of a public trade) in the Phase 1 ending logic.
note.src: FRUS XI d87; cmc/oct26/doc5; FRUS XVI d384·d386; Phase 1 ending logic D

HM-H5.time: 9 a.m. (4 a.m. in Washington, 11 a.m. in Moscow)
HM-H5.place: Admiralty House, on the telephone to Paris and Bonn
HM-H5.title: Europe with One Voice
HM-H5.clock: 6 hours until the Moscow broadcast (3 p.m. London time)

telegram.subject: General de Gaulle’s reply
telegram.text: General received Prime Minister’s message last night and saw me this morning. / General said: France has not opposed blockade, and if Soviets press Americans in Berlin France will act with United States. But France was informed, not consulted, and will not sign joint declaration on decision on which it was not consulted. / France will add no word to any bargain trading European bases for Cuba; such a bargain would only show that America has no will to defend Europe. / General added at end that if British Prime Minister wishes to speak in name of Europe, he must first come into Europe. I take this to refer to Brussels negotiations.

HM-H5.event: Last night you were in touch with Paris and Bonn, proposing that the three countries take a common position: Europe’s missiles are not to be bargained against Cuba. Adenauer agreed at once. The 86-year-old chancellor makes no secret of his fear, ever since the Berlin Wall, that America might sell Europe out. De Gaulle’s answer came in the morning: France would act with the United States but would not sign a joint paper. In Washington they had spent the night drafting a reply to Khrushchev’s “knot” letter, and in Moscow Khrushchev was getting ready to put his second letter out over the radio.
HM-H5.scene: You did not smile as you read de Gaulle’s cable. To speak in the name of Europe, first come into Europe: that means the Common Market negotiations, now dragging on in Brussels for ten months. Will you issue an Anglo-German declaration without France? Adenauer says go ahead regardless. Lord Home says a declaration by two countries alone would be read inside NATO as Britain and Germany standing up to America, and that is just the crack Khrushchev wants. And there is another way: write a proposal for talks into the declaration, giving Europe a mediator’s seat. Six hours remain until the Moscow broadcast at 3 p.m., and though you do not know it, that broadcast will mention the missiles in Turkey. At the very moment Europe’s bases become a bargaining chip, the voice Europe speaks with will be the one settled this morning.

voices.who: De Gaulle (Paris, as reported by Ambassador Dixon)
voices.text: France has not opposed the blockade, and if the Soviets put pressure on the Americans somewhere like Berlin, France will act with the United States. But we will not sign a joint declaration on a decision on which we were not consulted. If the British Prime Minister wishes to speak in the name of Europe, he must first come into Europe.
voices.src: FRUS XI d46 (based on the gist of Acheson’s report of 10/22)

voices.who: Adenauer (Bonn, as reported by Ambassador Steel)
voices.text: Prime Minister, ever since 13 August 1961 I have feared that America might bargain Europe away. The moment you put the missiles in Cuba and the missiles in Europe on the same scales, Berlin goes on those scales next. Even if France will not sign, our two countries must do it.

A declaration by two countries alone will be read inside NATO as Britain and Germany standing up to America. That is exactly the crack Khrushchev wants. If you issue one at all, do it after America has decided, and in the form of support for America. Issue it first and you narrow America’s options, and the President will not forget it.

choices.text: Issue an Anglo-German declaration without France, in two sentences: Europe’s missiles are not for bargaining, and the two countries support America’s decision
choices.why: The judgment that Europe must draw the line before anyone utters the word “trade”
choices.after: The declaration went out at noon, from London and Bonn at once. When Radio Moscow spoke of the missiles in Turkey three hours later, the Anglo-German declaration read like an answer written a day in advance. Washington was neither grateful nor angry. Inside the White House, those who had been discussing a trade held up the declaration and said, “Europe is already against it.”

choices.text: Drop the declaration: one without de Gaulle would only open a crack, so wait today for America’s decision and support it afterward
choices.why: The judgment that a Europe that is not three is not one
choices.after: Adenauer was disappointed, and the Bonn papers wrote of “London’s hesitation.” When Radio Moscow read out Khrushchev’s second letter at 3 p.m., you called in your senior ministers. What Britain does in that room is now Britain’s decision alone.

choices.text: Write a proposal for a three-power summit into the Anglo-German declaration: Europe refuses a trade, but will offer a place for the talks in Europe
choices.why: The reckoning that refusal alone leaves no way out, so Europe must become the place where the way out is found
choices.after: The declaration went out at noon, and at 3 p.m. Radio Moscow spoke of the missiles in Turkey. That night, through TASS, Khrushchev said he would “study the proposal of London and Bonn carefully.” Washington made no comment. At 11 p.m. Ormsby-Gore telephoned to explain what that silence meant.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. On 22 October de Gaulle told Acheson that he did not oppose the blockade and would act with the United States over Berlin, and he is known to have said that he had been informed but not consulted. Adenauer was informed by Ambassador Dowling. Britain’s negotiations to join the Common Market began in October 1961 and were vetoed by de Gaulle in January 1963. There is no record that a joint Anglo-German-French declaration was considered at the time, and the cable is invented.

HM-H6.time: 10 a.m. (5 a.m. in Washington, 1 p.m. in Moscow)
HM-H6.place: Whitehall, the Prime Minister’s office behind the Joint Intelligence Committee room
HM-H6.title: The Price of Berlin

map.caption: Of the three land routes to West Berlin, one is the autobahn through the Helmstedt checkpoint.

HM-H6.clock: 29 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (3 p.m. on the 24th, London time)
HM-H6.event: On the night call you told the President to occupy Cuba and be done with it. At 10 a.m. the Joint Intelligence Committee heard Cooper’s briefing. Its conclusion matched what Lord Home said last night: Khrushchev’s most likely retaliation would be to cut off access to Berlin. White of MI6 judged that the Soviets had meant to come in November with a fait accompli and bargain over Berlin and the bases all at once. In Washington the President passed on your words at the morning meeting, and the Joint Chiefs confirmed again that preparing an invasion would take seven days. In Florida, 100,000 troops were already gathering.
HM-H6.scene: Lord Home and Thorneycroft are before you. Both have read the record of last night’s call. Thorneycroft reports on the state of the three battalions of the Berlin garrison and the 55,000 men of the British Army of the Rhine. If the routes are blocked, the LIVE OAK plan first tests the way with a small armed convoy, then a breakthrough in division strength, then the selective use of nuclear weapons. Britain has been part of that plan since 1959. Lord Home makes a different point. If word goes round Washington that the Prime Minister told the President to occupy Cuba, the advocates of invasion will carry it about with them. And once an invasion begins, Khrushchev will try to pay it back in Berlin rather than lose in Cuba. In the 1948 blockade you were an opposition MP, and you remember how the airlift held out for eleven months. The Soviets had no bomb then. You must decide whether to take back last night’s words or see them through.

voices.who: General Strong (director of the Joint Intelligence Bureau, gist of a later report to the Prime Minister)
voices.text: The Americans were ready to go it alone, without consulting their allies, or whatever their allies said. If the Russians struck back in Berlin over action in Cuba, the U.S. government was prepared to see action begun in Cuba run all the way to nuclear war.

Prime Minister, what you said last night is a gift to the hawks in America. Even the British Prime Minister wants an occupation, they will say. Once an invasion begins, Khrushchev cannot afford to lose in Cuba, so he will pay it back in Berlin, and then the British Army of the Rhine stands in the front line. Take it back now and the President will understand. He said himself last night that it would take a week.

The first stage of LIVE OAK is a platoon-sized convoy. If that is stopped, next comes a division, and after that, nuclear weapons. The British Army of the Rhine goes into that second stage. If you are telling the Americans to use force, Prime Minister, then the force Britain will put up in Berlin has to be settled the same day.

choices.text: Do not take back last night’s words: order preparations for LIVE OAK stage one, and confirm to the President that in Berlin Britain stands with America
choices.why: The judgment that firmness taken back a day after it is spoken is weakness itself
choices.after: On Saturday, 27 October, the night America’s preparations for air strikes became public, Soviet forces stopped Allied vehicles bound for West Berlin at the Helmstedt checkpoint. The two crises overlapped. A LIVE OAK convoy stood on the autobahn, and the British Army of the Rhine went on alert. Khrushchev answered not in Cuba but in Berlin.

choices.text: Send the President a message tonight correcting last night’s words: the blockade is the right first step, and Britain will quietly strengthen its preparations for Berlin
choices.why: The reckoning that for Britain, safety in Berlin matters more than force in Cuba
choices.after: The message went that evening, and the President replied with brief thanks. Ormsby-Gore reported that word was going round the White House that “the Prime Minister was overexcited last night.” You let it stand. At 6 p.m. it is time to show Gaitskell the photographs.

choices.text: Since an invasion would take seven days, urge air strikes to destroy the missiles first: the Cuban question must be settled before a counterblow comes in Berlin
choices.why: The reckoning that if time is on Khrushchev’s side, better to cut time short
choices.after: The President did not reply, but on the evening of 23 October the Joint Chiefs put the air-strike plan forward again. After the U-2 was shot down on 27 October, the scales in the White House tipped. Before dawn on the 29th the first formations took off from airfields in Florida. How much the British Prime Minister’s words weighed in that decision, no one can measure.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In the call of 23 October Macmillan asked about occupation and spoke of “enough force at the start,” but he did not recommend occupation. LIVE OAK was the U.S.–British–French Berlin contingency planning organization set up in April 1959 (under Norstad’s command); some 55,000 men in the British Army of the Rhine and three battalions in the Berlin garrison are the usual figures for the early 1960s. That British intelligence saw a Berlin blockade as the most likely Soviet retaliation is in the Cooper report. The Soviet Presidium records contain no plan for a Berlin blockade; Ending H is a premise built only on the fears expressed in Western documents.

epilogues.A: In the House of Commons on 30 October, Macmillan called it the week in which a “super-Munich” had been avoided, and in December at Nassau he obtained Polaris missiles from Kennedy. In January 1963 de Gaulle vetoed Britain’s entry into the Common Market, and in August the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed in Moscow, the very treaty he had written of in his letter of 28 October. He resigned through illness in October 1963, and his diary of the Cuban week was not published until 2011.
epilogues.B: London was informed on the day the air strikes began. How far the British prime minister’s advice to the President on the morning of 23 October weighed in the White House, no one knows. The British Army of the Rhine went on alert against the closing of the Berlin corridors, and the House of Commons was recalled in emergency session.
epilogues.D: The public trade ended the crisis a day sooner, and the British prime minister went down in the record as the man who built the bridge. But Ankara did not forgive Britain, Adenauer turned his back on Britain’s voice inside NATO, and in January 1963 de Gaulle added one more line to his reasons for refusing Britain the Common Market: “Britain is a broker between America and the Soviet Union.”
epilogues.E: The three-week standstill became two months, and the talks in London or New York spread to Berlin, bases and disarmament, and dragged on. Britain won a seat at the table, but afterward Washington used the private line less often.
epilogues.F: A London conference the Americans did not attend became an Anglo-Soviet conference, and the missiles in Cuba stayed “for the duration of the talks.” When the next crisis came, in Berlin in the spring of 1963, Britain was neither America’s ally nor the Soviet Union’s counterpart.
epilogues.H: On the day the Berlin corridors were closed, the British Army of the Rhine went to LIVE OAK phase one, and the two crises, Cuba and Berlin, overlapped. Whether what the British prime minister said on the private line on the night of 23 October was the first step down that road is a question historians would ask later.

dossier.t: Born in London in February 1894, the son of a publisher, he is 68 in October 1962. He served as an officer in the Grenadier Guards in the First World War and was wounded three times; the bullet wounds to his pelvis and thigh on the Somme in September 1916 kept him in hospital and under the surgeon for years, and left their mark on his walk and on one hand. Elected for Stockton in 1924, he saw the misery of an area of mass unemployment, and in the Munich division of October 1938 he was one of the few who, with Churchill, refused to support the government. At Suez in 1956, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, he was hawkish at first, but when the pound collapsed and he saw that America held the purse strings he swung toward withdrawal, and in January of the following year he succeeded Eden as prime minister. In February 1959 he visited Moscow and spent ten days with Khrushchev, and that year he won a sweeping general election. He speaks slowly and obliquely, has a habit of reaching for history and the classics, and is known as a man who hides his nerves behind the appearance of an Edwardian gentleman. His wife Dorothy, whom he married in 1920, is a daughter of the Duke of Devonshire; from about 1929 she carried on a long affair with the Conservative MP Robert Boothby, and you did not divorce her but kept the marriage.

Lord Home, foreign secretary since 1960, is a Scottish peer, quiet and firm, and more suspicious of the Soviet Union than you are. Ormsby-Gore, the ambassador in Washington, is your own choice, sent out in 1961; he has been Kennedy’s friend since their London days in the 1930s and is in and out of the President’s family homes, so he hears what is said inside the White House before any other ambassador. Your private secretary de Zulueta handles foreign affairs and is the man who comes in carrying the box of telegrams; your principal private secretary, Bligh, keeps the record of meetings. Butler, First Secretary of State and in effect deputy prime minister, was a Munich man as under-secretary at the Foreign Office in 1938; he lost the contest for the premiership to you in 1957 and is still thought, within the party, to have his eye on the succession. On 13 July you dismissed seven ministers in a single night, the Chancellor, Selwyn Lloyd, among them, and since then there has been talk in the party that the prime minister is on shaky ground. The American ambassador, Bruce, calls on you often, but finds it humiliating that the big news from Washington reaches you on your private line before it comes through embassy channels.

His greatest fear is that Britain becomes a country that is informed of American decisions but not consulted. The lesson of Suez was that no British foreign policy works without America, which is why he counts the private relationship kept up with Kennedy by teleprinter and telephone since the inauguration as British diplomacy’s greatest asset. The future of Britain’s nuclear force hangs on America’s Skybolt air-launched missile, and the 60 Thor missiles on British soil are under a dual-key system, one key American and one British. He fears that Khrushchev will use Cuba as a bargaining counter over Berlin, and having lived through the blockade of 1948 and the Wall of 1961, a war over Berlin is the thing he most wants to avoid. At home, the negotiations on Common Market entry have been stuck in Brussels for ten months; Labour’s Gaitskell came out against entry at his party conference in early October; and since the rout in the Orpington by-election in March there has been talk in the party of changing the prime minister. His hope is that the crisis ends with American power forcing the Soviet Union to back down, and leads on from there to a test ban agreement and disarmament talks.

movers.intro: Whether Macmillan’s eight days actually entered into Kennedy’s decisions, or whether Britain was an ally that was merely informed, is an old debate in the history of British diplomacy. Even after the records of the private-line calls were released, the verdicts did not converge. The main views are these:
views: Len Scott: holds that Britain was informed after the decisions rather than consulted on them, and that it is hard to find any trace of Macmillan’s advice changing Washington’s choices. Yet the nightly calls gave Kennedy a trusted counterpart with whom to sort out his thinking, and in that sense, he judges, Britain’s place was real and not symbolic.

Alistair Horne: writes in the official biography that Macmillan regarded this week as the tensest of his premiership, and took the very fact that Kennedy telephoned every day as a measure of British influence. He sees the proposal to freeze the Thors and the open letter to Khrushchev as Macmillan’s attempts to break out of the role of listener.

Nigel Ashton: describes the Kennedy–Macmillan relationship as interdependence, but an interdependence tilted to one side. Over Cuba Britain backed the American decision from behind, and in return won Polaris at Nassau in December; in that sense, he argues, the crisis was bound up with the future of Britain’s nuclear force.

John Gearson: points to Macmillan’s consistent preference for negotiation and the avoidance of war in the Berlin crisis, and holds that in the Cuban week, too, what he feared most was not Cuba but Berlin. The warnings against a Berlin bargain, from his first reply on 22 October to the call of 26 October, were on this reading a continuation of the same line.
movers.note: The calls of 24 and 27 October do not survive in the American records, so parts of the account rest on Macmillan’s memoirs and his later-published diary. The Thor passage in the call of 26 October reads differently in different transcripts.
